name: Dagbani
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Dagbani (dagb1246) is not in the catalog. The single sweep item, Lewis 1999 'Rhythmic ambiguity in the Dagbamba drumming of Ghana', is an unpublished BA Honours thesis in ethnomusicology (University of New England; Glottolog keyword 'Drum communication'; language code auto-assigned from 'dagbamba') — not about word stress, no copy located, priority none. Using material already saved from the earlier pass plus a StressTyp2 v1 check, the picture is: Fisch 1912 (pp. 3-4, first-hand, German) reports the main stress 'mostly on the antepenult', often shifted to the penult by heavy syllables, while conflating it with high tone; Olawsky 1999/2002 claim regular penultimate stress per phonological word (with a final-stress subset) — seen only in Google Books snippets and second-hand citations, full texts unobtainable (LINCOM print; CUP chapter 403; JALL 2004 paywalled); Hudu 2007/2010 (UBC, bot-walled) measured no duration/intensity difference for Olawsky's 'stressed' vowels; Inusah 2021 (pp. 157-158, on file) and Hudu 2022 (pp. 274, 287, on file) treat Dagbani as a non-stress tone language. Dagbani has no StressTyp2 v1 record. Best first-hand statement read: Hudu 2022 'a non-stress language like Dagbani'. Highest-priority unobtained sources: Olawsky 1999/2002 (the penult-stress claim) and Hudu 2010 (the acoustic refutation). all lookups were by direct URL/API. Files and updated under

new_statements.quote: Olawsky (1999) was the first to claim that Dagbanli marks stress which is largely predictable in the language and notes that Dagbanli stress is correlated with a higher amplitude and longer duration; distinct from tone. On the contrary, (Hudu 2007) shows that the vowels which Olawsky described as stressed are neither longer in duration nor higher in intensity than vowels that are supposed to be unstressed. This assertion supports the widely held view among many linguists (e.g. Hudu 2010) that Dagbanli like other Mabia languages is not stress marking.

On the contrary, (Hudu 2007) shows that the vowels which Olawsky described as stressed are neither longer in duration nor higher in intensity than vowels that are supposed to be unstressed. This assertion supports…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The literature is split. The reference grammar (Olawsky 1999; also Olawsky 2000, 2002) analyses Dagbani as a tone language that additionally has predictable word stress, one main stress per phonological word, normally on the penultimate syllable (a small subset of words with final stress), cued by amplitude/duration rather than pitch — available to me only via snippets and reports. Native-speaker phonologists reject this: Hudu (2007, 2010) found no duration/intensity correlate and Hudu 2022 calls Dagbani 'a non-stress language' (with a trochaic bimoraic foot motivated by segmental phonotactics, whose head 'does not bear stress'); Inusah 2021 concludes Dagbanli 'is not stress marking'. The oldest description, Fisch 1912:3–4, put the 'Starkton' mostly on the antepenult, shifting to the penult when that syllable is heavy, and noted the stressed syllable always carries high tone.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described in the accessible sources; Riemer 2010 (summarising Olawsky 2002) speaks only of counting 'main stresses' per phonological word.
new_statements.exceptions: Per snippets of Olawsky 2002 (via Taylor ed. 2015:231): 'a subset of words with final stress'; Olawsky 2000: 'Heavy syllables do not automatically attract stress'. Fisch 1912: negative prefixes bi/ku and imperative -má attract the accent, infinitive -bu/-gu pushes it to the antepenult, adverbial yi- 'scatters' it over all syllables; compounding and suffix loss shift it.
new_statements.domain_note: Olawsky's stress is a property of the phonological word (used as his wordhood diagnostic: one main stress per p-word, incl. suffixed words and compounds). Hudu 2022's prominence is foot-level headedness (left-headed bimoraic trochee inside the prosodic word = root + inflectional suffix), explicitly not stress. All statements concern words in isolation; no phrase-level claims.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Dagbani (dagb1246). Inusah 2021 is explicitly cross-dialectal (Eastern/Tomosili, Western/Nayahili, Nanunli). Hudu's work draws mainly on the Eastern dialect. Fisch 1912 describes 'Dagbane' as spoken in North Togo and the northern Gold Coast (eastern Dagbon area, early 20th c.). Olawsky's data (1999/2002) are reported second-hand only.

new_statements.quote: Thus, while the more prominent syllable does not bear stress, the structure of the prosodic foot under discussion in this paper displays other relevant properties of a trochaic foot in stress languages. [...] In stress languages, the primary indicator of headedness within the prosodic foot is stress. [...] In a non-stress language like Dagbani, headedness can only be determined using these other (non-prosodic) criteria.
new_statements.citation: Hudu, Fusheini. 2022. Defining the prosodic word with segmental processes in Dagbani. Acta Linguistica Academica 69(3): 271-300. doi:10.1556/2062.2021.00437
new_statements.reading: Dagbani is a tone language without word stress: the leading present-day Dagbani phonologist treats it explicitly as a non-stress language whose left-headed moraic (trochaic) foot is diagnosed by segmental criteria only. This agrees with Inusah 2021: 157-158 (on file), which reports Hudu's 2007 acoustic finding that Olawsky's 'stressed' vowels are neither longer nor more intense and concludes 'stress does not exist in the phonology of the language'. The competing claim of regular penultimate stress (Olawsky 1999, 2002; the basis of the old StressTyp [P] label) was seen only in Google Books snippets. The earliest first-hand placement statement, Fisch 1912: 3-4 (on file), gives 'mostly antepenultimate, frequently penultimate with heavy syllables' but explicitly conflates stress with high tone. For a catalog entry, the defensible coding is 'no word stress (tone language); a penultimate-stress analysis (Olawsky 1999) exists but was refuted acoustically (Hudu 2007/2010)'.

sources.quote: Thus, while the more prominent syllable does not bear stress, the structure of the prosodic foot under discussion in this paper displays other relevant properties of a trochaic foot in stress languages. [p. 274] ... In a non-stress language like Dagbani, headedness can only be determined using these other (non-prosodic) criteria. [p. 287]
sources.note: First-hand, peer-reviewed: Dagbani is explicitly treated as a non-stress language; prominence within the (trochaic, left-headed, moraic) foot is established by segmental criteria (sonority, place licensing), not stress. Silent on Olawsky's penult claim by name.

sources.quote: Ich beschränkte mich, die Silbe mit dem Starkton durch einen Akzent zu bezeichnen. Diese Silbe hat wohl stets den hohen Ton. Die stark betonte Silbe ist im Dagbane meist die drittletzte, doch bewirken die folgenden Silben, Präfixe und Suffixe, mannigfache Verschiebungen. Es scheint, wie im Griechischen, der Unterschied zwischen schweren und leichten resp. kurzen und langen Silben auf die Stellung des Akzents einen starken Einfluß auszuüben. Silben mit gedehnten oder auch mit weiten Vokalen, mit Diphthongen und ferner mit h, gb, kp, ny wirken als schwere, durch sie kommt der Akzent häufig auf die zweitletzte Silbe zu stehen.
sources.note: pp.3–4 'Töne': marks the 'Starkton' syllable with an accent; 'Die stark betonte Silbe ist im Dagbane meist die drittletzte' (mostly antepenultimate), but heavy syllables (long/open vowels, diphthongs, ŋ, gb, kp, ny) often draw the accent to the penult; some affixes attract or repel it (neg. bi/ku, imperative -má attract; infinitive -bu/-gu pushes it to the antepenult); the stressed syllable 'hat wohl stets den hohen Ton'.
